_note: Section 7 drafts by reader 75 (cannabis edibles and concentrates), for a targeted second reading

tasks.locator: Abstract; Results, 1st (unlabelled) paragraph; Methods › Study Participants and Coding, paragraph; Methods › Measurements, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Chart review of all emergency visits to one Colorado university hospital, 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2016: 449,031 eligible visits, 9,973 with a cannabis-related diagnosis code, 2,567 (25.7%) judged at least partly attributable to cannabis. Route was recorded in 2,432 (94.7%): 238 edible (9.3%) and 2,194 inhaled; the 135 visits with insufficient documentation were counted as inhaled, giving 2,329. A dose was recorded in 130 (5.1%). Route came from the nursing assessment questionnaire and the providers' notes, and inhalation was presumed when it was not documented. Visits attributable to inhaled and to edible cannabis both rose each year (Figure 2, an image, not read).

tasks.locator: Table 2; Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 2nd paragraph; Abstract
tasks.extracted: Table 2, edible-attributed (n = 238) against inhaled-attributed (n = 2,329) visits, % (difference in percentage points, 95% CI): intoxication 48.3 vs 27.8 (20.5; 13.9 to 27.1); acute psychiatric symptoms 18.0 vs 10.9 (7.1; 2.1 to 12.1); cardiovascular symptoms 8.0 vs 3.1 (4.9; 1.4 to 8.4); any psychiatric symptom 26.1 vs 24.5 (1.6; -4.2 to 7.4); gastrointestinal symptoms 15.1 vs 32.3 (-17.2; -22.1 to -12.2); cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4 vs 18.0 (-9.6; -13.5 to -5.7). The text adds that severe adverse cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and ventricular dysrhythmia, occurred in both groups; no counts are given. Only two route groups appear in the tables and text, edible and inhaled; the inhaled group is not broken down by product, and tobacco mixed into joints is not recorded.

tasks.locator: Table 2, counts; Results › Reasons for Cannabis-Attributable ED Visits, paragraph
tasks.extracted: Table 2 counts, edible and inhaled: intoxication 115 and 647 (762 in all); acute psychiatric symptoms 43 and 254 (297); cardiovascular symptoms 19 and 73 (92); gastrointestinal symptoms 36 and 752; cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 20 and 420. Editors' arithmetic: edible-attributed visits were 15.1%, 14.5% and 20.7% of the intoxication, acute psychiatric and cardiovascular visits, so most visits for those reasons were inhaled-attributed. Across the 2,567 visits (reasons not mutually exclusive): gastrointestinal symptoms including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 788 (30.7%; 301 people accounted for 440 visits), intoxication 762 (29.7%), psychiatric symptoms 633 (24.7%), cardiovascular symptoms 92 (3.6%).

tasks.locator: Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Discussion, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Edible-attributed against inhaled-attributed visits: women 51.3% vs 33.1%; living outside Colorado 40.8% vs 6.6%; admitted 18.9% vs 32.9% (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (0 to 121); age similar, no figures. Table 1, all 2,567 attributable visits: median age 30; 65.2% male; 9.8% from outside Colorado; 31.6% admitted, 62.5% discharged, 2.1% transferred to a psychiatric facility, no deaths. The Discussion says the higher admission rate in the inhaled group seemed driven by admission of patients with cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; this is not analysed.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors write that, although less frequent overall, edible products lead to more acute psychiatric events and cardiovascular symptoms than inhaled exposure, and that the high frequency of visits and the greater likelihood of admission with inhalable products suggest that education about the adverse health effects of inhalable cannabis may have the greatest effect on public health.

tasks.locator: Results › Colorado Sales Data by Route of Exposure; Table 3; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Colorado sales, 2014 to 2016 (Table 3): 219 edible-attributed and 1,819 inhaled-attributed visits, so edibles were 10.7% of attributable visits, against 0.32% of THC sold by weight (flower 327,990 kg at an assumed 20% THC; 21.2 million edible units at an assumed 10 mg each; ratio of flower to edible THC 309, range 279 to 325). The authors call the observed share about 33 times higher than expected if both routes were equally toxic and say careful interpretation is required: THC content was assumed, one hospital was compared with state-level sales, home-grown and black-market cannabis were not counted, and sales are not geocoded.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Abstract (Limitation)
tasks.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: retrospective design with exposure captured largely through self-report; no comparative community-based exposure cohort; patients presenting to the emergency department differ from the overall population of people who use cannabis, most of whom may have no adverse effects, so a prospective cohort of people who use cannabis and people who do not is needed; doses could not be verified and ingested doses may have been larger than inhaled doses. A dose was documented in 80 edible-attributed visits and in 19 it was 50 mg or higher; the authors were surprised by the low edible doses reported, given the THC content of a typical Colorado joint. Route was presumed inhaled when not documented, which they say could have biased the analyses toward greater toxicity in the inhaled group. The hospital has the second most visits per year in the state and is in an area of high cannabis availability.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Timing as described by the authors, citing a pharmacology review (Grotenhermen 2003, not read): inhaled cannabis gives clinical effects within 10 minutes, a peak blood concentration within 30 to 90 minutes and complete clearance within 4 hours; oral THC does not reach a significant blood concentration until at least 30 minutes, peaks at about 3 hours and clears about 12 hours after ingestion. People report longer-lasting effects with edibles than with smoking or vaping (reference 8, a consumer survey) and more intense effects and unpleasant psychiatric symptoms (reference 9, an analysis of Twitter posts); neither was read. Death has been associated with edible products in three cases taken from news reports (references 10 to 12). No timing was measured in this study's patients.

tasks.locator: Methods › Role of the Funding Source, paragraph; Grant Support, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Funded by a competitive grant from the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment for a project on the adverse health effects of edible cannabis products; the paper states that the department was not involved in study design, analysis, data interpretation or dissemination. The first author received support from NIH K23 GM110516, NIH CTSI UL1 TR001082 and CDPHE 17 FHHA 96950 (Grant Support). Disclosures: the first author reports grants from the department during the study and sits on the Colorado Retail Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee, a group of clinicians and scientists reviewing the literature on the public health effects of cannabis; another author reports department grants; authors not named disclosed no conflicts. No cannabis-industry, tobacco-industry or advocacy funding is printed.

tasks.locator: Abstract; Introduction, paragraph
tasks.extracted: A narrative overview published as an RTI Press occasional paper, written for the educated layperson and policy makers. The Abstract says little research has evaluated how ingestion differs from other methods of cannabis use in therapeutic efficacy, subjective effects and safety; that the most prominent difference is the delayed onset with ingestion; and that consumers who do not understand this may consume more than intended before the effect starts, often resulting in profoundly adverse effects (no count is given). The Introduction says the authors describe promises and challenges and critically examine extant research; no search method, selection criteria or appraisal of studies is described.

tasks.locator: Overview of Edibles, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: In Colorado in 2014, 1.96 million units of edible medicinal cannabis-infused products and 2.85 million units of edible retail products were sold, which the authors say accounted for about 45 percent of the total cannabis sales in the state (a state report, as cited); the measure of sales is not stated. Homemade edibles are not tracked, and the data show sales and not the proportion of people who consume edibles.

tasks.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: After eating, liver first-pass metabolism forms 11-OH-THC, a potent psychoactive metabolite that appears in blood in higher quantities after ingestion than after inhalation (as cited); the authors write that it may be responsible for the stronger and longer-lasting effect of edibles compared with comparable doses of smoked cannabis. Inhaled THC takes initial effect within minutes, peaks in about 20 to 30 minutes and tapers within 2 to 3 hours; the initial effect of edibles takes 30 to 90 minutes and the high is longer-lasting, with a peak 2 to 4 hours after ingestion (Grotenhermen 2003 and others, as cited, not read). Weight, metabolism, sex and eating habits are said to affect how soon and how long.

tasks.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 5th paragraph
tasks.extracted: After oral doses, plasma THC is lower than after smoking or infusion, and its correlation with degree of intoxication varies considerably across individuals (Hollister 1981, as cited); oral bioavailability is 6 to 10 percent of the amount in the product (Schwilke 2009, as cited). The authors say the lack of consistency and the delayed intoxication may lead both new and experienced people to take more than intended, and write that edible products are responsible for the majority of health care visits due to cannabis intoxication, which they attribute to a failure to appreciate the delayed effects (a 2015 viewpoint by Monte, Zane and Heard, as cited, not read).
tasks.quote: responsible for the majority of health care visits due to cannabis intoxication

tasks.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 7th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Dosage estimation for retail products may be inexact (Vandrey 2015, as cited). Anecdotal reports from medicinal cannabis patients are said to confirm that even people who take cannabis daily may consume more than expected (Hudak 2015, a case report, as cited): having eaten the suggested serving first, patients ate the entire product after not feeling any effects, and found it practical to eat the entire product in one sitting.

tasks.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 14th paragraph
tasks.extracted: One death after an edible is described: in March 2014 a 19-year-old man died of injuries from jumping from a fourth-floor balcony in Colorado after eating a cannabis-infused cookie (a public-health case report, as cited). The text says he was told to eat one serving, and that having not felt intoxicated within 60 minutes he ate the whole cookie within 2 hours of that serving; the autopsy identified cannabis intoxication as a chief contributing factor.

tasks.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 19th paragraph
tasks.extracted: A 2014 newspaper investigation found the actual THC content of retail edibles often differed significantly from labels; from mid-2014 Colorado required THC to be tested and labelled but tested only against a threshold, which does not check label accuracy. One study of medicinal edibles sold in California and Washington is reported to have found that the total THC content of 83 percent of edibles tested differed from the labelled amounts by over 10 percent, with more than half containing significantly less than claimed and nearly a quarter significantly more (Vandrey 2015, as cited; not read).

tasks.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 10th, 11th and 12th paragraphs; reference list (Kim 2016)
tasks.extracted: Children: poison-centre calls about cannabis in the United States rose 30.3 percent a year in decriminalized states, 11.5 percent in states in transition and 1.5 percent in states without legal change, 2005 to 2011 (Wang 2014, as cited), with similar increases in edible-related calls in 2013 to 2015 (Cao 2016, as cited). The authors write that emergency visits for child exposure remain relatively low: a Colorado children's hospital saw no accidental edible ingestions in 2005 to 2009, eight children in 2013 and 14 in 2014 (a hospital-association web item, as cited). Visitors: out-of-town patient visits to an Aurora, Colorado hospital for problems after edibles almost doubled from 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits between 2013 and 2014, with no significant difference for Colorado residents (Kim 2016, as cited; not read); that study's authors attributed the rise to higher potency and visitors' unfamiliarity with edibles. The reference list gives the letter's authors as Kim, Hall, Genco, Van Dyke, Barker and Monte (the first author of Monte 2019 is Monte).

tasks.locator: Promises of Edibles, 10th and 11th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: On smoke: cannabis and tobacco smoke are said to be similar in kind in toxicity; cannabis smoke is linked to lung inflammation and bronchitis; the link to chronic lung disease is unclear; epidemiological research links habitual smoking to several cancers but is complicated by small samples and co-occurring tobacco smoking. The authors then write that eating edibles does not seem to affect lung function or raise cancer risk, calling this a solid rationale for choosing the route. No study of people who eat cannabis is cited for the last point.

tasks.locator: Acknowledgments; author-information panel
tasks.extracted: Preparation of the manuscript was supported by RTI International internal funds and National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA-03672. All eight authors are at RTI International. No conflict-of-interest statement is printed in the manuscript, and no cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are declared.

tasks.locator: Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Baseline Appointment, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Experimental Appointment, paragraph
tasks.extracted: Adults aged 21 to 70 who had used cannabis at least four times in the past month and had used, at least once, the strongest product that could be assigned (24% THC flower or 90% THC concentrate) with no adverse reaction; no other non-prescription drug in the past 60 days, no daily tobacco, light alcohol use. Within each form, participants were randomly assigned by random-number table to a labelled strength (flower 16% or 24%; concentrate 70% or 90%), bought it at a local dispensary that set allotments aside for the study, used it freely for 5 days, and on the fifth day used it in their preferred way at home before a mobile-laboratory visit; measures were taken before use, about 13 minutes after use and 1 hour after use. The form itself was each person's own choice.

tasks.locator: Results › Descriptive Information, paragraph; Abstract; Table 1
tasks.extracted: 133 people were assessed (64 in the flower group, 69 in the concentrate group). Twelve were excluded because blood THC after use was below 0.02 µg/mL (study mean 0.24), taken to mean they had not used the product at home as instructed, leaving 121 (55 flower, 66 concentrate, so 9 and 3 were left out from the two groups; editors' arithmetic); mean age 28.8 and 28.3 years; 42% and 48% women in Table 1 (the Abstract gives 46% and 45%). Table 1: concentrate group glass rig or tube 92% and hash pen 8%; flower group pipe 51%, bong 31%, vaporizer 11%, joint 7%.

tasks.locator: Results › Cannabinoids, paragraph; Table 2; Figure 1
tasks.extracted: THC and 11-OH-THC peaked at the short-term post-use assessment and then fell. Mean blood THC after use was 0.32 µg/mL in the concentrate group and 0.14 µg/mL in the flower group (printed as SE 0.43 and 0.16 in the Abstract and Results; the Discussion gives them as standard deviations). THC and 11-OH-THC were consistently higher in the concentrate group across assessments, including before use (Table 2, THC 0.01, 0.32, 0.03 against 0.004, 0.14, 0.02; 11-OH-THC 0.004, 0.011, 0.008 against 0.001, 0.005, 0.004 µg/mL); form effect for THC F(1,228) = 11.00, P < .01. The text reports no effects of labelled strength within a form on blood levels.

tasks.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: Self-rated intoxication, the marijuana effects scale, tension and vigor peaked at the short-term assessment and decreased by 1 hour. Intoxication did not differ by form (form effect P = .11; means 0.08, 2.40, 1.93 in the flower group and 0.14, 2.35, 1.63 in the concentrate group); the marijuana effects scale did not differ by form (P = .18); tension (P < .01) and vigor (P < .001) were lower in the concentrate group across assessments. No associations with labelled strength are reported in the main text.

tasks.locator: Results › Neurobehavioral Performance › Cognition, paragraph; Table 2; Figure 3
tasks.extracted: Delayed verbal recall errors rose after use in both groups (linear effect P < .001; flower 0.65, 2.21, 1.88; concentrate 0.90, 1.50, 2.33 before, short-term and 1 hour after); form effect P = .65, form by quadratic time P = .02 (above the set threshold). Inhibitory control and working memory scores rose over the session, which the authors suggest may reflect practice; inhibitory control was higher in the flower group across all assessments, with no short-term change and no association with labelled strength.

tasks.locator: Results › Neurobehavioral Performance › Balance, paragraph; Table 2; Discussion, 5th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Eyes-closed sway rose after use and returned to its pre-use level by 1 hour in both groups (quadratic time P < .001; form effect P = .85). Eyes-open balance showed a trend (P = .05) that did not meet the a priori threshold; the eyes-closed head-back condition showed no change from before to after use. The authors describe about an 11% increase in sway with eyes closed, which they say is consistent with effects of moderate alcohol (as cited).

tasks.locator: Table 1; Results › Descriptive Information, paragraph; Methods › Baseline Appointment, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: At baseline, concentrate group against flower group: concentrate use on 16.5 against 3.5 of the past 30 days; flower use on 15.4 against 20.6 days; regular use begun at 17.7 against 20.0 years; baseline THC-COOH 0.087 against 0.044 µg/mL; product used at the session 0.11 g against 0.22 g. Between the two strength groups within each form there were no differences except in race among the concentrate groups (P < .01), and none in the amount used.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors write that there was no within-form association of labelled strength with blood levels, suggesting that people may titrate toward similar THC exposure as strength rises. For similar intoxication despite higher blood THC they offer greater tolerance in the concentrate group, receptor saturation, and individual differences in metabolism or sensitivity, and say future research must test them.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Limitations, paragraph
tasks.extracted: Ethical limits precluded random assignment to concentrate or flower, so pre-existing differences between the groups may partially account for the findings; there was no placebo control because such products do not exist on the legal market; federal rules restricted control over dosing and masking to product strength; interactions of cannabinoid strength and ratio, mode of use, expectancies and technique were not tested.

tasks.locator: Conclusions, paragraph; Key Points › Meaning
tasks.extracted: Delayed recall and balance impairment were associated with short-term use even in regular consumers; people who used concentrates showed similar or lower subjective intoxication and short-term impairment than people who used flower; THC exposure was much higher in the concentrate group, prompting concern about long-term clinical and neurobehavioral implications. The Key Points say concentrates were associated with higher THC exposure and potentially greater risk. Long-term and clinical outcomes were not measured.

tasks.locator: Author-information panel (Conflict of Interest Disclosures; Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor); Methods › Baseline Appointment, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Funding: NIH grant DA039707 (Hutchison) and Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment grant 96947 (Bidwell); the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation or the decision to submit. Disclosures: Bidwell reports grants from NIH/NIDA and the State of Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment; Ellingson NIH; Klawitter the department and NIH; Sempio the department and NIH; Bryan NIH and the State of Colorado; no other disclosures. Participants bought their assigned products at one local dispensary that set allotments aside for the study; no payment from the dispensary is declared.

tasks.locator: Results, 1st (unlabelled) paragraph; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Data Sources and Searches
tasks.extracted: Seven databases were searched (October 2021, updated July 2022; English language and human studies only) for human studies of any design that reported a THC concentration in any unit or a product from which a high concentration could be inferred. Searches identified 49,729 unique records, 5,828 full-text reports and 452 included studies: 225 observational studies, 142 randomized trials, 51 case reports and 34 case series. The earliest was published in 1971 and 60% (269) in 2017 to 2022.

tasks.locator: Results › Potential for Evidence Synthesis, paragraph
tasks.extracted: Of 452 studies, 54 (12%) examined a direct association between concentrates and a health outcome and 189 (42%) a direct association between THC concentration and an outcome; 114 (25%) examined an indirect association between THC concentration and outcomes and 62 (14%) an indirect association between concentrates and outcomes; 212 (47%) had a control group; effect estimates were reported in 184 (41%), measures of precision in 274 (61%), significance tests in 335 (74%) and raw data in 232 (51%).

tasks.locator: Results › Exposures, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Most studies concerned generic cannabis types (284, 63%); products typically high in concentration (oils, concentrates, hash, extracts, skunk, resins) were examined in approximately 2% to 10% of all studies. When THC was given as a percentage (172 studies, 349 exposures) the median was 12% (mean 17.4%, range 0% to 100%, interquartile range 3.6% to 24%); when given in milligrams (113 studies, 143 exposures) the median was 15 mg (mean 37.4, range 0.3 to 500, interquartile range 7.5 to 26). Units and indices varied.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Concentrations Studied, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Market strengths the authors cite from other sources: a 2018 survey of products sold in 7 US states found most products between 15% and 30% THC; in Colorado the average THC of flower assayed rose from 14% to 19% between 2014 and 2020 and that of concentrates from 46% to 68%. They describe the median of 12% studied as well below what is currently on the market and say the low strengths studied are likely due to the restriction of research cannabis in the United States to a federal supply that lacks concentrates.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Exposure Assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Study Selection Criteria › THC concentration of products, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors write that most studies failed to capture all the elements of cannabis use needed to estimate exposure dose, and recommend that studies at least report THC concentration, product used, frequency of use and route, in THC units that can be standardised. They state that THC concentration is not the same as dose.

tasks.locator: Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Funding and interests in the included studies: 24% (109) did not report a funding source and 32% (143) did not report whether authors had conflicts of interest; 25 studies (6%) were funded by the cannabis industry and 58 (13%) had an author who disclosed a financial tie with the industry.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Conclusions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion › Limitations, paragraph; Abstract
tasks.extracted: Conclusions: the review supports strong conclusions about the usefulness of the literature for characterising risks and benefits of the current marketplace; there are serious limitations in the generalisability of the studies to the current marketplace or to the people who buy its products; high-quality evidence on whether THC concentration should be regulated is scarce. Limits: searches were sensitive rather than specific; relevant studies may have been missed despite AI-assisted screening; heterogeneity of designs did not allow risk-of-bias assessment of individual studies; incomplete and inconsistent reporting left gaps in the extracted data.

tasks.locator: Acknowledgments, 1st paragraph; Conflicts of Interest, paragraph; Introduction, 2nd paragraph (PMC shows it under the Plain-Language Summary heading as its 3rd paragraph)
tasks.extracted: Funded by the State of Colorado under House Bill 21-1317, which asked the Colorado School of Public Health for a review of the physical and mental health effects of high-potency THC marijuana and concentrates; the funder was not involved in the design, conduct or publication of the paper. As printed: one author is a paid consultant as conflict-of-interest advisor for Health Canada, including its cannabis committees; one is a paid author for UpToDate for a chapter on cannabis intoxication; one has research funding from the Institute of Cannabis Research (Colorado State University) and serves on the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment's Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed.
